nameStory: The Formosa lily gets its name from Taiwan's former name, Formosa, meaning 'beautiful' in Portuguese. Portuguese sailors coined this name for Taiwan in the 16th century, and this stunning lily is indeed a beautiful native of that island nation.
description: The Formosa lily is a tall, elegant bulb plant that produces spectacular trumpet-shaped white flowers with a sweet fragrance. Originally from Taiwan, this lily has escaped from gardens and naturalized in a few scattered locations across the world, though it's extremely rare in New England with only one recorded observation. It can grow 3-6 feet tall with sturdy stems lined with narrow leaves and topped by large, showy blooms that face outward rather than drooping.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Large white trumpet-shaped blooms up to 6 inches long that face outward horizontally, with a sweet, intoxicating fragrance especially strong in evening. The petals curve back slightly at the tips and have a waxy, smooth texture.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged alternately up the stem, dark green with smooth edges and a slightly waxy feel. They're densely packed along the stem, getting smaller toward the top.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, sturdy single stem rising 3-6 feet from an underground bulb, with flowers clustered at the top. The stem feels firm and slightly ridged when gently squeezed.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Upright seed capsules that split open to reveal flat, papery seeds with thin wings. The capsules feel dry and brittle when mature, rattling softly when shaken.

habitat: Extremely rare in New England, found only in disturbed areas where it has escaped from cultivation. When it does establish, it prefers well-drained soils in sunny to partially shaded locations, often near old garden sites or along roadsides where bulbs may have been discarded.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from bulbs in late spring, growing rapidly into tall stems with developing leaves.
seasonality.summer: Spectacular white trumpet flowers bloom in mid to late summer, with peak fragrance in evening hours.
seasonality.fall: Seed capsules ripen and split open, releasing winged seeds. Foliage begins to yellow and die back.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back completely to underground bulb, leaving no above-ground trace.

funFact: This lily is so intensely fragrant that in its native Taiwan, the perfume is strongest at dusk to attract night-flying sphinx moths as pollinators, and a single flower can scent an entire garden from 50 feet away!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with Easter lily, but Easter lilies bloom in spring and have broader leaves. The outward-facing flowers and intense evening fragrance help distinguish Formosa lily from other white lilies.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called Formosa lily, Taiwan is no longer known as Formosa, but the plant keeps this historical name. It's sometimes sold as 'Taiwanese lily' in modern nurseries, which is more geographically accurate.
compareHints: Unlike our native Canada lily and Turk's-cap lily which have drooping, downward-facing flowers, Formosa lily blooms face outward horizontally. It differs from tiger lily by being pure white without spots, and from wood lily by having trumpet-shaped rather than upward-facing cup-shaped flowers. The intense sweet fragrance is much stronger than any of our native lilies.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's true lilies, Canada lily is the only one with consistently downward-facing, bell-shaped flowers in yellow to orange shades.
Unlike its relatives Canada lily and Turk's-cap lily which have downward-facing or nodding flowers, wood lily is the only native lily in New England that consistently faces its flowers upward.
Among New England's lilies, tiger lily is the only one with black bulbils in the leaf joints and the only non-native species commonly encountered.

Among New England's native lilies, Turk's-cap lily is the tallest and most dramatic, with its hanging orange flowers and completely recurved petals setting it apart from the upward-facing Canada lily and the smaller, red Wood lily.
Among New England's true lilies, Michigan lily is distinguished by its moderate height (shorter than Turk's-cap lily but taller than wood lily) and its orange color with backward-curved petals.
Unlike our native lilies, martagon lily has distinctly whorled leaves rather than alternate or scattered leaf arrangements.
